title: Astronaut Joshua Kutryk's wife gives birth while he's aboard the International Space Station
summary: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is once again a proud father — only this time, he's beaming from space.

image.caption: Joshua Kutryk touches his pregnant wife Heather Kutryk's belly ahead of the launch at Kennedy Space Center on Oct. 1, 2026 in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is once again a proud father — only this time, he's beaming from space.
Sometimes missing your kid's birth is okay, if you're on a mission aboard the International Space Station

His wife Heather Kutryk gave birth to a baby girl on Tuesday, the Canadian Space Agency announced. Joshua Kutryk is currently aboard the International Space Station, as part of the seven-crew-member team of Expedition 75.

"The birth of a child is one of life's most meaningful milestones, and welcoming our daughter into the world is a true blessing for our family," the couple said in a statement from the Canadian Space Agency.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives."
Joshua Kutryk will return to see his new baby in March 2027. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
The little girl, whose name has yet to be publicly announced, is the couple's third child. Their other two kids are ages seven and five.

"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," the couple said.
In an interview with CBC before leaving for space, Kutryk admitted missing the birth would be difficult, but it was something they were prepared for.

"This is a significant challenge, a big adventure. But we've both always liked adventure to some respect, liked challenge. Certainly I feel that if anyone was to do this, it would be us. If anyone was to do it successfully, my wife, my family are just amazing," he said at the time.

And it was a good time for their newborn to arrive. If it wasn't for the fact that a newborn's vision is still very much developing, she would be able to see her dad's place of work flying through the sky.
When going to space means missing the birth of your child 🚀
It will still be a while before Kutryk trades spacewalks for diaper duty. He's scheduled to return home in March 2027.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited," said the couple.
Philip Drost is a network senior writer for CBC News based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.
